notes.4: A common incorrect answer was C, which is the opposite of the correct answer. Candidates should be encouraged to learn the meaning of these terms carefully.
notes.8: The area under a speed-time graph gives the change in distance, but the two animals here did not start at the same position. Many weaker candidates forgot the initial separation of 100 m, and this led them to choose D.
notes.10: The key point that candidates needed to realise was that the graphs show only the motion between the bounces. The horizontal component of the velocity is constant, so C is correct. Some candidates chose D, which would have been the correct shape for the vertical component.
notes.11: This question was found to be relatively difficult. A common mistake was to choose D, which is the upward force F divided by the mass m. The upward force is not the resultant force because the rocket has weight. The correct equation is F – mg = ma and solving this gives C.
notes.19: This question can be answered by determining the pressure at the boundary between the oil and the water. The pressures exerted by the oil and by the water at this boundary must be equal. The pressure of the oil is 30.0ρ oilg and the pressure of the water is (30.0 – x)ρ waterg. Solving this gives x = 4.5 cm.
notes.34: Careful working is needed to answer this question. The resistances of the lamps can be determined from the ratings and the question states that these resistances are constant. Lamp P has a resistance of (250 2 / 50 =) 1250 Ω and lamp Q has a resistance of 312.5 Ω. They are connected in series so they have the same current, and therefore power ∝ resistance. The power in lamp P is four times the power in lamp Q.
notes.35: A popular incorrect answer was B but this would allow the clock to operate the cooling system when the thermostat switch is open (i.e. the house is already cold). The clock and thermostat switches must be in series for normal operation of the system.
notes.36: When the circuit is working correctly, there is a p.d. of 110 V between S– and C1. Faults B, C and D would each cause the p.d. between S– and C1 to fall to zero.
notes.37: Candidates found this question difficult and it requires careful working. The currents in the three ‘horizontal’ resistors are 8 A, 3 A and 1 A; the corresponding potential differences are 8 V, 3 V and 1 V. The currents in the three ‘vertical’ resistors are 5 A, 2 A and 1 A; the corresponding potential differences are 5 V, 2 V and 1 V. The total current in the supply is 8 A and the potential difference V is 13 V.
notes.general_comments:
The time constraint of one hour does make the paper a challenge: it demands quick and accurate working by
candidates. The average time of 90 seconds per answer is made possible by having many questions that can
be answered after a quick (but careful) read through the question.
Candidates should be advised never to spend a disproportionately long time on any one question. They
should also be advised to use the spaces on the question paper for their working. Care with units is essential.
Prefix errors are a cause of many wrong answers as are corresponding power-of-ten errors.
Questions 1, 2, 20, 23 were the easiest questions on the paper. Candidates found Questions 19, 34, 36 and
37 difficult.
